title: Floyd: City of Blinding Lights
directAnswer: Answer many shortest-path queries on a directed weighted graph. Precompute all-pairs shortest paths once with Floyd-Warshall: a triple loop over an intermediate node k that relaxes dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). After the O(V³) precompute, every query is an O(1) table lookup; report -1 when the entry is still infinity (unreachable). Crucial: the k loop must be outermost.

remember.pattern: All-pairs DP: relax through each intermediate node k
rules: The **k loop is outermost** — k is the set of allowed intermediates. Swapping the loop order gives wrong answers.
**Guard against INF overflow**: only relax when both `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` are finite (or use a sentinel safely below MAX).
The graph here is **directed** — set `dist[u][v]` only (not the reverse) when reading an edge.
Keep the **minimum among parallel edges** when initializing: `dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)`.
After the precompute, each query is **O(1)**; an entry left at INF means **unreachable → -1**.
whenToUse: **Many** shortest-path queries between arbitrary pairs on a **small** graph (V ≤ ~400–500)
All-pairs distances are needed, not just from one source
Dense graph where a per-query Dijkstra would repeat work
Negative edges allowed (no negative cycle) — Floyd-Warshall still works
antiSignals: Single source, one query → Dijkstra is O((V+E) log V), far cheaper than O(V³)
Large V (thousands+) → V³ is too big; run Dijkstra per source/query instead
Unweighted graph → BFS per source beats the cubic precompute
Need the actual path, not just the distance → store a 'next' matrix for reconstruction
remember.takeaway: Floyd-Warshall is dynamic programming over 'which intermediate nodes are allowed': after considering nodes 1..k as possible waypoints, dist[i][j] is the best path using only those. Adding node k either helps (route i→k→j) or doesn't. The cubic precompute pays for O(1) queries — the right trade when queries are many and the graph is small.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize a many-queries all-pairs setting as Floyd-Warshall, can state the DP meaning of the loops, get the k-outermost loop order right, and handle unreachable pairs and overflow.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Putting the k loop inside (wrong answers), letting INF + INF overflow, treating a directed graph as undirected, or running a fresh Dijkstra per query when there are too many queries.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the loop order via the DP invariant ('after iteration k, dist[i][j] uses only intermediates ≤ k'), justify Floyd over per-query Dijkstra by the query count and small V, and mention the negative-cycle diagnostic (any dist[i][i] < 0).

problemStatement:
You are given a directed weighted graph of `n` nodes (labeled `1` to `n`) with edges `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` meaning a directed road from `u` to `v` of length `w`. Then you are given `q` queries; each query `(a, b)` asks for the **length of the shortest path** from `a` to `b`.

For each query, return the shortest distance, or `-1` if `b` is unreachable from `a`.
constraints: The graph is directed; parallel edges may appear (keep the minimum)
understanding: Roads are one-way (directed), and there can be a huge number of queries against the same fixed graph. That ratio — small graph (n ≤ 400), many queries (up to 10⁵) — is the signal to precompute all shortest paths once and answer each query by lookup. Floyd-Warshall fills a distance matrix where dist[i][j] becomes the shortest path from i to j. Its loops encode a DP: after allowing nodes 1..k as intermediate stops, dist[i][j] holds the best route using only those waypoints; finishing all k means full freedom of intermediates. Unreachable pairs stay at infinity and are reported as -1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the roads directed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. An edge [u, v, w] sets dist[u][v] = w but not dist[v][u]. Treating it as undirected would invent paths.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many queries, and how big is the graph?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁵ queries on n ≤ 400. That favors an O(V³) precompute (~6.4 × 10⁷) plus O(1) lookups over per-query Dijkstra.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if a node can't reach the target?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Report -1. Its matrix entry stays at the infinity sentinel.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be parallel edges between the same pair?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — keep the minimum weight when initializing the matrix.

examples.explanation: 1→2 = 5 direct. 3→1 has no path (nothing points to node 1) → -1. 1→4 = min(24 direct, 1→2→4 = 5+6 = 11) = 11.

approaches.name: Per-Query Dijkstra (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention this first: 'each query is a single-source shortest path, so run Dijkstra from the query's source'. Then note it repeats work when queries are many.
hints: Each query (a, b) is just a single-source shortest path from a. What's the standard tool for non-negative weights?
Run Dijkstra from a, then read dist[b]. Weights are positive here, so Dijkstra is valid.
If queries are few this is great; if there are 10⁵ queries you may re-run Dijkstra from the same source repeatedly — wasteful, motivating an all-pairs precompute.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each Dijkstra is O((V + E) log V). Doing it per query is O(q · (V + E) log V). With q up to 10⁵ and a dense graph (E ≈ V²), this balloons; caching results per distinct source helps but Floyd-Warshall is cleaner when queries hit many sources.
approaches.explanation:
A query asks one source-to-target distance, which is exactly what Dijkstra computes.

**Per query.** For query `(a, b)`, run Dijkstra from `a`: seed `dist[a] = 0`, pop the closest unsettled node from a min-heap, relax its outgoing edges. When done, return `dist[b]`, or `-1` if it stayed infinite.

**Why it's correct.** Weights are non-negative, so Dijkstra's greedy 'settle nearest first' is valid and yields exact shortest distances from `a` to every node — in particular to `b`.

**Why it can be wasteful.** With up to 10⁵ queries spread over many sources, you may run full Dijkstra runs that recompute overlapping information. Memoizing by source bounds it at `V` runs, but when the graph is small and queries are many, one O(V³) precompute that answers *every* pair in O(1) is simpler and often faster overall.
approaches.insight: Per-query Dijkstra is the right instinct for one-off shortest paths, and it scales to large graphs where V³ is impossible. The decision hinges on the query count and graph size: many queries on a small graph flips the economics toward all-pairs precomputation.

approaches.name: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution for many queries on a small graph. Phrase it as 'precompute every pair's shortest path with a triple loop, k outermost, then answer each query in O(1)'.
hints: Queries hit many different sources. Instead of one source at a time, can you compute the shortest path between every pair up front?
Build an n×n matrix: dist[i][j] = edge weight (min over parallels), 0 on the diagonal, infinity otherwise. Then improve it by allowing intermediate stops.
For each candidate intermediate node k (outer loop), every pair (i, j) can try routing i→k→j: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). After all k, the matrix holds all shortest paths.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Initialization is O(V² + E). The triple loop is O(V³) = 400³ ≈ 6.4 × 10⁷ — fast in both Java and Python-with-care. Each of the q queries is an O(1) lookup, so total O(V³ + q). Space is the O(V²) matrix.
approaches.explanation:
When queries are numerous and the graph is small, computing all pairs once beats per-query work.

**The DP meaning.** Let `dist_k[i][j]` be the shortest path from `i` to `j` using only nodes `1..k` as intermediate stops. With no intermediates allowed (`k = 0`), it's just the direct edge (or infinity). Adding node `k` as an allowed waypoint gives two choices: ignore it (keep `dist_{k-1}[i][j]`) or route through it (`dist_{k-1}[i][k] + dist_{k-1}[k][j]`). Take the min. After `k = n`, all nodes are allowed and `dist[i][j]` is the true shortest path.

**Why the k loop is outermost.** `k` indexes the DP layers — the set of permitted intermediates. The invariant 'after iteration k, every entry uses only intermediates ≤ k' holds only if we finish all `(i, j)` updates for a given `k` before moving to `k+1`. Because the in-place update `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])` reads row `k` and column `k`, and those entries are not improved further within the same `k` iteration (a shortest path through `k` doesn't use `k` twice), updating in place is safe. Put `k` inner and you allow paths that revisit intermediates inconsistently — wrong answers.

**Overflow guard.** Initialize unreachable entries to a sentinel and only relax when both `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` are finite; otherwise `INF + INF` can overflow or create bogus 'shorter' paths. Using a large-but-safe sentinel (well under MAX/2) or an explicit finite check both work.

**Answering queries.** Each `(a, b)` is `dist[a][b]`, or `-1` if it's still the sentinel. Directed edges set only `dist[u][v]`; parallel edges keep the minimum.
approaches.insight: Floyd-Warshall is DP over a third dimension you don't store — the allowed-intermediate set. The triple loop with k outermost literally builds shortest paths layer by layer. The same matrix, with a tiny tweak (replace +/min by OR/AND), computes transitive closure (reachability) — and `dist[i][i] < 0` after the run flags a negative cycle.

pitfalls: Putting the k loop anywhere but outermost — produces wrong distances.
Letting INF + INF overflow — use a sentinel below MAX/2 or guard with a finite check.
Initializing the matrix as undirected on a directed graph.
Returning the sentinel value instead of mapping it to -1 for unreachable pairs.

commonMistakes: Placing the k (intermediate) loop inside i/j instead of outermost.
Integer overflow from adding two infinity sentinels.
Returning the infinity sentinel rather than -1 for unreachable pairs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: k indexes the DP layer (allowed intermediates). It must be the outermost loop so all (i, j) pairs are updated for a given k before k advances. Putting k inside lets paths use intermediates inconsistently and yields wrong distances.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Infinity overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If unreachable is Integer.MAX_VALUE, then dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] can overflow to a negative number that looks 'shorter', corrupting the matrix.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE;
// dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] overflows when both are INF
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4;   // headroom
if (dist[i][k] == INF) continue;        // and/or skip infinite rows

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Directed graph read as undirected
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each road is one-way. Mirroring edges invents reverse paths, so a query like 3→1 (truly unreachable) would wrongly return a finite distance.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)
dist[v][u] = min(dist[v][u], w)   # invents a reverse road
commonMistakesDetailed.good: dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)   # directed: only u -> v

followupVariations.title: Bellman-Ford Shortest Path
followupVariations.hint: Single source with negative edges; also detects negative cycles (Floyd flags them via dist[i][i] < 0).

followupVariations.title: Dijkstra: Shortest Reach 2
followupVariations.hint: Single-source non-negative shortest paths — the right tool when V is large or queries share a source.

followupVariations.title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors
followupVariations.hint: Direct Floyd-Warshall application: all-pairs distances, then count reachable nodes within a threshold.

followupVariations.title: Transitive Closure / Reachability
followupVariations.hint: Same triple loop with OR/AND instead of min/+ to compute which pairs are connected.

patternNote: Canonical All-Pairs Shortest Path via Floyd-Warshall. Recognize it when many shortest-path queries hit a small (V ≤ ~400) graph, or when you need every pair's distance. The triple loop is DP over allowed intermediate nodes with k outermost; the same skeleton computes transitive closure and detects negative cycles. For large V or single-source queries, prefer Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford.
